summary:
Tunisia criminalises same-sex conduct under Penal Code Article 230, which carries up to three years' imprisonment. The provision dates from the 1913 Penal Code, was largely modified in 1964, and covers both male and female same-sex activity, rendered in Arabic as "Liwat" and "El Mousahaka". Enforcement is active rather than dormant, and authorities use the anti-sodomy law to detain and question people about their sexual activities and orientation.

Article 226, which outlaws "outrages against public decency", is applied to gender expression. Cross-dressing is not expressly illegal, but transgender people, alongside gay people, are frequently accused under this article.

Amnesty International reported on 11 February 2025 that at least 84 people, mainly gay men and transgender women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. A mass conviction on 31 October 2024 imposed prison terms of up to four and a half years, which an appeal court upheld on 5 February 2025; four of those convicted were released after sentence reduction.

Human Rights Watch documented at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over the six months to 29 March 2016, all convicted under Article 230. Interviewed detainees reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police.

Anal examinations are used as evidence in these prosecutions and refusal is treated as evidence of guilt. In June 2017 a 16-year-old was sentenced to four months in jail for homosexuality after refusing an examination. Two men arrested in Sousse on 7 December 2016 on suspicion of homosexual activity were subjected to anal probing and forced to sign confessions of sodomy, then received eight-month prison sentences on 11 March 2017 while on bail. In a case reported on 6 July 2020, two men arrested on 3 June on suspicion of same-sex conduct were subjected to an attempted anal examination and were sentenced for homosexuality.

In September 2017 the interior minister, Mehdi Ben Gharbia, agreed to stop forced anal tests, stating that examinations could no longer be imposed by force, physically or morally, or without consent. Courts continued ordering anal tests throughout 2018 and 2019. Tunisia also pledged to the United Nations in 2017 to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases while retaining the anti-gay law itself, and a local outlet warned at the time that the pledge decriminalised nothing.

Recorded enforcement totals were 56 people jailed in 2016, 79 in 2017 and 127 in 2018, with at least 22 arrests by April 2019. These are raw counts without a per-capita denominator, so they measure enforcement volume rather than comparative risk.

Legal gender recognition is unsettled and is granted or refused court by court, and gaps persist. The Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man in April 2023 after weighing contradictory lower-court judgments, including case No. 12304/2018, and finding no consistent precedent below the Court of Cassation. A separate Tunis Court of First Instance ruling holds that gender identity disorder is a psychological condition that permits legal change of sex.

Transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings. The Intersection Association described this in November 2024 as systemic identity refusal beginning at detention and continuing through the prison system.

Cairo 52 records the October 2021 arrest of two transgender women under morality and debauchery provisions.

No shelter, victim-protection, medical care, custody, facility-access or other protection machinery specific to transgender visitors is described in the sources.
tangentialFactors:
Official statements recorded in the sources address homosexuality or sexual orientation rather than transgender people: they include opposition to same-sex marriage, support for punishing homosexuals, and official descriptions of homosexuality as perversion or illness requiring treatment. No documented official statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically appears in the inventory.

Reports of family rejection, violence in public spaces, violence within families and suicides among LGBTQ Tunisians are described in the sources as common, but without figures or a stated period, so their scale and recency cannot be established from this record.

The 2017 commitments on forced anal testing illustrate reform by pledge without legal change: the anti-sodomy statute was retained, and courts kept ordering examinations after the interior minister's undertaking.

Enforcement figures for same-sex conduct are reported as raw annual totals only. Without population or arrest-rate denominators they cannot be used to rank Tunisia against other jurisdictions.
localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition for transgender residents is decided case by case with no settled rule. On 22 December 1993 the Court of Appeals in Tunis rejected a trans woman's request to change her legal gender from male to female, declaring her gender change a "voluntary and artificial operation" that did not justify a change in legal status.

In 2018 a trans man succeeded in changing his legal status in what is described as a revolutionary judgement, while the Tunis Court of First Instance refused recognition to a transgender man in April 2023, citing contradictory lower-court judgments including case No. 12304/2018 and the absence of consistent precedent below the Court of Cassation. A separate first-instance ruling treats gender identity disorder as a psychological condition permitting legal change of sex. Recognition therefore turns on the forum, and Cairo 52 records that gaps persist.

Identity refusal continues inside the prison system. The Intersection Association reported in November 2024 that transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender across detention records, arrest processes and court hearings, which it characterised as continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system.

LGBTQ Tunisians face legal and social discrimination, and the sources record family rejection, violence in public spaces, violence within families and suicides without figures or dates.
outOfScopeNotes:
No transgender-specific provisions on detention procedures, identity documents beyond civil status change, screening, facilities, custody, care or protection machinery are stated in the sources; the absence of such provisions in this record is not evidence that none exist.

The date of the Court of First Instance ruling holding that gender identity disorder permits legal change of sex is not given in the source, so it cannot be placed relative to the April 2023 refusal.

Whether the September 2017 undertaking against forced anal testing remains in force is unresolved. Courts are documented ordering examinations through 2018 and 2019, and no later ruling on the practice appears in the inventory.

The sources give no trans-specific violence statistics with denominators for Tunisia, so no comparison against the general homicide rate can be drawn from this record.

The inventory contains no documented statement about societal tolerance of transgender people specifically; the tolerance figures and official positions it carries address homosexuality or sexual orientation generally.
